title: Caste, Gender and the Texts
bigQuestion: How have Hindu texts been used to support and to challenge hierarchies of caste and gender, and how have Hindus themselves responded?

story.title: A Fire at Mahad
story.kicker: In 1927 a lawyer holds a public burning of an old law book, and the argument has not stopped.
paragraphs: On December 25, 1927, in the town of Mahad in western India, thousands of people gathered at a conference. Earlier that year many of them had marched to a public water tank, the Chavdar Tale, to drink from it. By law the tank was open to all, but people from communities treated as untouchable had long been kept away. After they drank, some upper-caste residents performed rites to "purify" the water.

The conference was led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, a lawyer and scholar who had grown up in a Mahar family and faced untouchability all his life. That evening, a copy of the Manusmriti, an ancient Sanskrit law book, was placed on a pyre and burned. Ambedkar's followers explained that they were burning the rules that had denied them dignity, not attacking all of Hinduism.

The act shocked many Hindus. Some were angered that a sacred law book was burned. Others, including some Hindu reformers, agreed that the Manusmriti's rules on caste and on women could not guide a modern society. Many Dalits still mark December 25 as Manusmriti Dahan Din, the day of the burning of the Manusmriti.

Almost a century later, the questions raised at Mahad are still debated in India and among Hindus in the United States. What do the texts actually say about caste and gender? Which texts carry authority, and for whom? How have saints, reformers and scholars answered?

This chapter studies those questions historically. It names the passages, the people who used them, and the many Hindus who pushed back from inside and outside the tradition. It describes each position in terms its holders would recognize, and it does not issue a verdict on Hindus or on Hinduism.
story.think: Burning a book is a strong symbol. What did it mean to the people at Mahad, and why might other Hindus have seen it differently?

lessons.title: Two Different Words
lessons.mainIdea: Varna names the four classes in the texts; jati names the many birth communities of lived social life.
reading: English uses one word, caste, for two different Sanskrit ideas. *Varna* means the four classes named in the texts: Brahmins (priests and teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (farmers and merchants) and Shudras (laborers and servants). Varna is a textual and ideal scheme that appears first in Rig Veda 10.90.12.

*Jati* means "birth" and names the thousands of real communities, often linked to a traditional occupation, region and language, into which people were born and within which they married. Historians note that jatis were numerous and varied, and that how they ranked themselves differed from place to place. Some jatis were placed outside the four varnas and treated as untouchable.

Scholars stress that the relation between the textual scheme and real life changed over time. British colonial censuses from 1871 onward tried to classify every jati in a fixed ranking, which some historians argue made caste more rigid. Understanding the difference between varna and jati helps students read the texts and the history accurately.

words.d: one of the four classes named in the texts
"birth"; one of the many real birth communities of Indian society
the practice of treating some groups as ritually impure and excluding them
an official count and classification of a population

look.title: Scheme and Society
look.text: Varna: four classes, named in texts, arranged in an ideal order. Jati: thousands of communities, tied to birth, work, region and marriage, whose ranking varied by place and time.
look.prompt: Why might it matter, in a history essay, whether a writer means varna or jati when they say "caste"? Give an example of a confusion that could result.

check.q: What does jati mean?
choices: One of the four ideal classes
check.why: Jati names birth communities; varna names the four classes.

check.q: Where do the four varnas first appear together?
check.why: The Purusha Sukta's verse 12 is the first list.

check.q: What do some historians argue about British censuses from 1871?
choices: They made caste more rigid by fixing rankings
check.why: Fixed colonial classifications may have hardened categories.

lessons.title: The Manusmriti
lessons.mainIdea: The Manusmriti is an ancient law book with strict rules on caste and women, and its authority has always been debated.
reading: The *Manusmriti*, or Laws of Manu, is a Sanskrit text on dharma credited by tradition to Manu, the first human. Scholars date it roughly to the 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE. It covers ritual, family life, kingship, law and punishment in about 2,700 verses. It belongs to smriti, texts "remembered" and ranked below shruti.

The Manusmriti sets strict rules by varna, with harsher punishments for Shudras than for others in some crimes, and it bars Shudras from Vedic learning. On women it contains verses that seem to pull in different directions. Verse 3.56 says the gods rejoice where women are honored. Verse 9.3 says a woman should be protected by father, husband and son and is not fit for independence.

Scholars note that the Manusmriti was one of many dharma texts and was not a code applied everywhere. It gained new weight under British rule, when colonial courts used it and similar texts to decide Hindu family law. Today many Hindus reject its caste and gender rules; some honor other parts of it; and critics like Ambedkar rejected it entirely.

words.d: an ancient Sanskrit law book on dharma, dated by scholars c. 2nd c. BCE–3rd c. CE
the genre of Sanskrit texts on dharma, law and duty
the right to be obeyed or followed; texts differ in how much authority readers give them

look.title: Two Verses on Women
look.text: Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice; where they are not honored, no rite bears fruit (3.56). Her father protects her in childhood, her husband in youth, her sons in old age; a woman is not fit for independence (9.3).
look.cite: Manusmriti 3.56 and 9.3, paraphrased from G. Bühler, The Laws of Manu (Sacred Books of the East 25, 1886)
look.prompt: How can both verses be in the same book? How might a traditional reader, a reformer and a feminist scholar each explain them?

check.q: How do scholars date the Manusmriti?
choices: The same year as the Gita Rahasya
c. 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE
check.why: Scholars place it in this broad range.

check.q: What does Manusmriti 3.56 say?
choices: The gods rejoice where women are honored
Women are not fit for independence
Shudras must not learn the Vedas
check.why: 3.56 is the verse on honoring women; 9.3 is on dependence.

check.q: How did British rule affect the Manusmriti's weight?
choices: Colonial courts used it for Hindu family law, raising its importance
check.why: Colonial courts gave dharma texts new legal weight.

lessons.title: Shambuka and Ekalavya
lessons.mainIdea: Two epic episodes, Shambuka in the Ramayana and Ekalavya in the Mahabharata, are central to modern debates about caste in the texts.
reading: In the Uttara Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, a Brahmin's young son dies, and the sage Narada says it is because a Shudra, Shambuka, is performing austerities, which the text treats as forbidden to his varna. Rama finds Shambuka and kills him, and the boy returns to life. Many scholars note that this episode is in the Uttara Kanda, which they judge to be a later part of the epic.

In the Adi Parva of the Mahabharata, Ekalavya, a tribal prince of the Nishadas, asks the teacher Drona to teach him archery and is refused. He makes a clay image of Drona and teaches himself before it, becoming a superb archer. When Drona learns of this, he demands Ekalavya's right thumb as his teacher's fee, so that Arjuna will remain the best archer. Ekalavya gives it.

Readers respond in many ways. Some devotees say these episodes must be understood within their own world, or note that some later retellings, such as Bhavabhuti's drama, grieve over Shambuka's death. Dalit and reformist writers read them as clear examples of caste injustice. Many teachers now tell Ekalavya's story to honor his skill and devotion while naming the wrong done to him.

words.d: a Shudra ascetic killed by Rama in the Uttara Kanda of the Ramayana
a Nishada prince who taught himself archery and gave his thumb to Drona
the fee or gift a student gives a teacher at the end of study
tapas; strict self-discipline for spiritual purposes

look.title: Retelling Ekalavya
look.text: Version A tells Ekalavya's story as a model of a devoted student. Version B tells it as a story of a teacher who wronged a gifted boy because of his birth. Version C honors Ekalavya's devotion and names Drona's act as unjust.
look.prompt: Which details from the Adi Parva does each version stress? Which version would you use to teach younger students, and why?

check.q: Who demands Ekalavya's thumb?
check.why: Drona demands it as his teacher's fee.

check.q: In which part of the Ramayana is the Shambuka episode?
check.why: Shambuka appears in the Uttara Kanda.

check.q: Why does Drona demand the thumb, according to the Adi Parva?
choices: So that Arjuna will remain the best archer
check.why: Drona had promised Arjuna he would be unmatched.

lessons.title: Basava and the Vachanas
lessons.mainIdea: Basava, a 12th-century Shiva devotee in Karnataka, rejected caste distinctions and founded a community of equal devotees.
reading: Basava, also called Basavanna, lived in the 12th century in what is now Karnataka. He was a minister at the court of Kalyana and a devotee of Shiva. With other poet-saints he composed *vachanas*, short prose poems in Kannada, which criticized empty ritual, temple wealth and caste pride.

Basava gathered a community, later called the Lingayats or Virashaivas, in which devotees of Shiva were to be treated as equals regardless of birth. Tradition says he supported a marriage between a family of Brahmin birth and a family of low-caste birth. The marriage provoked a violent backlash in Kalyana, and the community scattered.

One famous vachana contrasts the rich who build temples for Shiva with the poor devotee who has nothing, and says: my legs are pillars, my body the shrine, my head a cupola of gold. Basava's followers, today many millions in Karnataka and beyond, honor him as a saint and reformer. His vachanas are still sung and studied.

words.d: a 12th-century Shiva devotee and reformer in Karnataka
a short Kannada prose poem of devotion by Basava and other poet-saints
the community of Shiva devotees tracing its teaching to Basava

look.title: The Body as Temple
look.text: The rich will make temples for Shiva. What shall I, a poor man, do? My legs are pillars, the body the shrine, the head a cupola of gold.
look.cite: Basava, vachana, paraphrased from A.K. Ramanujan, Speaking of Siva (Penguin, 1973)
look.prompt: What does Basava replace the stone temple with? What does that say about who can worship?

check.q: What is a vachana?
choices: A short Kannada devotional prose poem
check.why: Basava's vachanas are Kannada poems.

check.q: Which deity was Basava devoted to?
check.why: Basava was a Shiva devotee.

check.q: What did Basava's community teach about birth?
choices: Birth decides who may enter heaven
Devotees should be equal regardless of birth
check.why: His community rejected caste distinctions among devotees.

lessons.title: Ravidas and Begampura
lessons.mainIdea: Ravidas, a bhakti poet from a leatherworking family, imagined a city without sorrow or caste, and his hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib.
reading: Ravidas, also spelled Raidas, was a bhakti poet of North India, usually dated to the 15th and early 16th centuries, who lived near Varanasi. He was born into a family of leatherworkers, a community treated as untouchable. He worked as a cobbler and became one of the most honored poet-saints of his age.

In one song Ravidas describes *Begampura*, "the city without sorrow," where there is no tax, no fear, no second-class or third-class people, and everyone may go where they please. Scholars read it as one of the earliest visions of an equal society in Indian literature. About forty of his hymns are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture.

Tradition says Mirabai, the Rajput princess-poet, honored Ravidas as her guru. Today the Ravidassia community, many of whom live in Punjab and in the diaspora, honors him as its founder, and temples to him stand in many countries, including the United States. His life shows how bhakti opened space for voices outside the Brahmin tradition.

words.d: a North Indian bhakti poet from a leatherworking family (c. 15th–16th c.)
"the city without sorrow"; Ravidas's vision of an equal society
the Sikh scripture, which includes about forty hymns of Ravidas

look.title: The City Without Sorrow
look.text: Ravidas (paraphrase): In the city without sorrow there is no grief, no tax, no fear, no second or third rank. Everyone walks freely. My friend, whoever lives there is a friend of mine.
look.prompt: What does Ravidas's city lack? Why would a poet who faced untouchability picture a city this way?

check.q: What does Begampura mean?
check.why: Begampura is Ravidas's city without sorrow.

check.q: Where are forty of Ravidas's hymns found?
check.why: The Sikh scripture includes his hymns.

check.q: Which poet-saint, by tradition, honored Ravidas as her guru?
check.why: Tradition links Mirabai to Ravidas.

lessons.title: Jyotirao Phule
lessons.mainIdea: Jyotirao Phule and Savitribai Phule opened schools for girls and lower castes and challenged Brahmin authority in the 1800s.
reading: Jyotirao Phule (1827 to 1890) was born in Pune into the Mali, or gardener, community. With his wife *Savitribai Phule* he opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, one of the first in India run by Indians. Savitribai became its teacher, facing insults and thrown mud on her way to work. The couple also opened schools for children of castes treated as untouchable.

In 1873 Jyotirao published Gulamgiri, "Slavery," which compared caste to slavery and dedicated the book to the American abolitionists. That year he founded the Satyashodhak Samaj, the "Society of Truth-Seekers," to work for equality. He read the Puranas and Vedic stories critically, arguing that they had been used to justify Brahmin power.

Phule influenced later leaders, including Ambedkar, who called him one of his three gurus, alongside the Buddha and the poet Kabir. Many Hindus admire the Phules as social reformers even when they read the texts differently. They are especially honored in Maharashtra, and Savitribai is remembered as a pioneer of women's education.

words.d: teacher and poet who, with Jyotirao Phule, opened a girls' school in Pune in 1848
"Slavery"; Jyotirao Phule's 1873 book comparing caste to slavery
the Society of Truth-Seekers, founded by Phule in 1873

look.title: The Phules' Work
look.cite: Standard biographical dates for Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule
look.prompt: Phule dedicated Gulamgiri to American abolitionists. What does that suggest about how he saw his struggle?

check.q: What did the Phules open in Pune in 1848?
check.why: Their girls' school opened in 1848.

check.q: What did Phule compare caste to in Gulamgiri?
check.why: Gulamgiri means slavery.

check.q: Whom did Ambedkar name as one of his three gurus?
check.why: Ambedkar named the Buddha, Kabir and Phule.

lessons.title: Mahad, 1927
lessons.mainIdea: At Mahad in 1927, Ambedkar led a march for water rights and a public burning of the Manusmriti.
reading: In March 1927 Ambedkar led thousands to drink from the Chavdar Tale, a public tank in Mahad, to assert a right already granted in law. This is called the *Mahad Satyagraha*. Afterward, some local residents held rites to purify the tank, and a court case over access followed for years.

On December 25, 1927, at a second conference in Mahad, the Manusmriti was burned. Ambedkar explained that the act was a protest against the rules that had denied his community dignity, education and equal rights. The burning, his followers said, was not an attack on all Hindus but on a code of inequality. The act was meant as a symbol, and it was read as one on every side.

Responses varied. Many orthodox Hindus condemned the act. Some reformist Hindus understood it even if they disliked the method. Gandhi, who opposed untouchability, did not endorse the burning. Among Dalits, the day became a symbol of self-respect. The event remains a key moment in the history of caste and scripture.

words.d: the 1927 march led by Ambedkar to drink from a public water tank in Mahad
an act that expresses a message through a symbol, not by force
a sense of one's own worth and dignity

look.title: Water, Then Fire
look.text: March 1927: thousands drink from a public tank their community had been kept from. December 1927: a law book whose rules had kept them from it is burned.
look.prompt: Why might the order of these two events matter? What did each act say, and to whom?

check.q: What was the Mahad Satyagraha about?
choices: The right to drink from a public water tank
check.why: It asserted access to the Chavdar Tale.

check.q: On what date was the Manusmriti burned at Mahad?
check.why: The burning took place on December 25, 1927.

check.q: How did Ambedkar describe the burning?
choices: As a protest against a code of inequality, not all Hindus
As a call to destroy all temples
check.why: He framed it as a protest against unequal rules.

lessons.title: The Constitution of 1950
lessons.mainIdea: India's Constitution, drafted under Ambedkar's leadership, abolished untouchability and guaranteed equality before the law.
reading: India's Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950. Ambedkar chaired its drafting committee. Article 14 guarantees equality before the law. Article 15 forbids discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 17 declares that untouchability is abolished and that its practice in any form is forbidden.

The Constitution also created *reservations*, a system of set-aside places in legislatures, government jobs and universities for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, to repair long exclusion. Laws such as the Protection of Civil Rights Act (1955) and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989) followed.

Many Hindus, including religious leaders, supported these reforms as true to their faith. Others resisted. Scholars and activists note that caste discrimination has not ended, in India or in some diaspora communities. The debate over caste has reached the United States, where some colleges and cities have considered or adopted caste in anti-discrimination policies, and Hindu American groups have disagreed about these steps.

words.d: the article of India's Constitution that abolishes untouchability
set-aside places in government, jobs and universities for historically excluded groups
the legal term in India for communities that faced untouchability

look.title: Law Against Caste Discrimination in India
look.cite: Constitution of India (1950); Protection of Civil Rights Act (1955); SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989)
look.prompt: Why might new laws have been needed after the Constitution already abolished untouchability?

check.q: Which article of India's Constitution abolishes untouchability?
check.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability.

check.q: What are reservations in India?
choices: Set-aside places for historically excluded groups
check.why: Reservations repair long exclusion.

check.q: Which statement about Hindu responses is accurate?
choices: The reforms were written by the British
Many Hindus supported the reforms; others resisted
check.why: Hindu responses varied widely.

lessons.title: Gargi and Maitreyi
lessons.mainIdea: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad shows two women, Gargi and Maitreyi, questioning the great teacher Yajnavalkya.
reading: In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, King Janaka holds a debate among learned Brahmins. The sage Yajnavalkya claims the prize. Among those who question him is *Gargi Vachaknavi*, a woman philosopher. In 3.6 she presses him with questions about what the world is woven upon, until he warns her not to ask too much.

In 3.8 Gargi returns and says she will ask two questions, like a warrior with two sharp arrows. Yajnavalkya answers with a teaching about the imperishable, akshara. Gargi then tells the assembly that no one will defeat him in debate. Readers note that she is both a challenger and a fair judge.

In 2.4 and 4.5, Yajnavalkya's wife *Maitreyi* asks him, as he prepares to leave home, whether wealth would make her immortal. When he says no, she asks for the knowledge that would. Many Hindu women scholars and teachers today point to Gargi and Maitreyi as evidence that women took part in the highest learning of the Upanishads.

words.d: Gargi Vachaknavi, a woman philosopher who questions Yajnavalkya in Brihadaranyaka 3.6 and 3.8
Yajnavalkya's wife, who asks for knowledge rather than wealth in Brihadaranyaka 2.4
a great sage and teacher in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad

look.title: Maitreyi's Question
look.text: Maitreyi asks: if this whole earth full of wealth were mine, would I be immortal by it? No, says Yajnavalkya; your life would be like the life of the rich, but there is no hope of immortality by wealth. Then Maitreyi says: what should I do with that by which I do not become immortal?
look.cite: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.2–3, paraphrased from F. Max Müller, The Upanishads, part 2 (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884)
look.prompt: What does Maitreyi's question show about what she values? Compare her choice to Nachiketa's in the Katha Upanishad.

check.q: Whom does Gargi question in the Brihadaranyaka?
check.why: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court.

check.q: What does Maitreyi ask for instead of wealth?
choices: The knowledge that leads to immortality
check.why: She says wealth cannot make her immortal.

check.q: How does Gargi compare her two questions?
choices: To two sharp arrows of a warrior
check.why: In 3.8 she likens her questions to arrows.

lessons.title: Mirabai and Modern Scholars
lessons.mainIdea: Mirabai defied custom out of devotion to Krishna, and today women scholars and chanters are reshaping the study of the texts.
reading: *Mirabai* was a 16th-century Rajput princess and poet devoted to Krishna. Her songs, in Rajasthani and Braj, tell of loving Krishna as her true husband. Tradition says her in-laws tried to stop her from singing and dancing in temples with holy people, and even tried to poison her, but she kept her devotion. Scholars note that many songs credited to her were composed later by others in her name.

Mirabai is loved across India. Her songs are sung in homes, temples and concerts, and she appears in films and comics. Readers see her in different ways: as a model of bhakti, as a woman who chose her own path, or both. Gandhi admired her courage and saw in her a model of gentle resistance.

In modern times many women have become Sanskrit scholars, professors of religion and teachers of Vedic chanting, roles once closed to them in many communities. Some traditional groups resisted this change; others welcomed it. Women scholars have also led new readings of figures such as Sita, Draupadi and Gargi, adding their voices to a very old conversation.

words.d: a 16th-century Rajput poet-saint devoted to Krishna
loving devotion to God
crediting a work to an author; many songs are attributed to Mirabai

look.title: Who Wrote Mira's Songs?
look.text: Hundreds of songs carry Mirabai's name in their last line. Scholars find that only some can be traced to early manuscripts; many were composed later by singers who took her voice. Devotees sing them all as Mira's songs.
look.prompt: Does it change a song's meaning if Mirabai herself did not write it? How might a scholar and a devotee answer differently?

check.q: Who was Mirabai?
choices: A 16th-century Rajput poet-saint devoted to Krishna
check.why: Mirabai sang of devotion to Krishna.

check.q: What do scholars note about songs credited to Mirabai?
choices: Many were composed later by others in her name
They are part of the Rig Veda
check.why: Scholars trace only some songs to early sources.

check.q: What change in the modern period does this lesson describe?
choices: Many women became Sanskrit scholars and Vedic chanters
check.why: Roles once closed to women opened to many.
